How should an investor divide wealth across assets that differ in expected
return, in volatility, and in how they move together? @markowitz1952 answered
that a portfolio cannot be judged asset by asset, because the risk of the whole
depends on the covariances between its parts as much as on the variances of
each. That observation turned portfolio choice into an optimization problem with
a closed-form solution, and it remains the point from which every later method
in this book departs.

This chapter is about **strategic allocation**: the portfolio an investor would
hold given long-run, unconditional beliefs about the assets, with no attempt to
time anything. We first derive the mean-variance problem and its two anchor
solutions, then implement them on the sixteen risky class series introduced in
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-theory, then ask what the resulting portfolios
actually bought and how much of it survives contact with data the optimizer had
not seen.

One warning before any number appears. Every moment in this chapter is estimated
on the **full sample**. Nobody standing at the start of the sample knew the
covariance matrix of its last year, so what follows is descriptive rather than
implementable, and
@sec-25-backtesting-theory does the honest version. The purpose here is to
establish what the textbook answer looks like when its inputs are not invented.

The data are the sixteen risky class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, and they enter in excess of the
Treasury bill, for the reasons given in
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: a tangency portfolio exists only
relative to a risk-free rate, `PortfolioAnalytics` has no argument for one, and
the excess formulation is the only one that stays coherent once weights are
allowed to sum to less than one.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
```
:::


## The Mean-Variance Problem {#sec-09-mean-variance-theory}

Write $\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathbb{R}^N$ for the vector of portfolio weights over
$N$ assets, $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ for the vector of expected excess returns, and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ for the covariance matrix of those excess returns. Let
$\boldsymbol{\iota}$ denote a vector of ones. The portfolio's expected excess
return and variance are

$$
\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad
\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}.
$$ {#eq-09-moments}

The second expression is the whole of @markowitz1952 in one line. The variance of
a portfolio is not the weighted average of the variances of its parts; the
off-diagonal terms of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ enter too, and they can be negative.
Combining assets can therefore produce a portfolio with a lower volatility
than any of its constituents, which is not true of any other portfolio
characteristic we use.

Two moments per portfolio make comparison a matter of geometry. In the plane
with volatility on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical, a
portfolio $A$ **dominates** a portfolio $B$ if
$\mu_A \geq \mu_B$ and $\sigma_A \leq \sigma_B$ with at least one inequality
strict: the same return for less risk, or more return for the same risk. This
is the mean-variance criterion of @markowitz1952, introduced in
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory, and it has a direction: a better
portfolio always lies to the northwest of a worse one. A portfolio that no
feasible portfolio dominates is **efficient**. The same vocabulary applies to
single assets, and @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation applies it to the
sixteen series before any optimizer runs.

An investor who cares only about these two moments therefore wants, for each
attainable level of expected return $\bar{\mu}$, the portfolio that achieves it
at least variance:

$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{w}} \; \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1,
\quad
\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} = \bar{\mu}.
$$ {#eq-09-problem}

The set of solutions, traced over $\bar{\mu}$, is the minimum-variance
frontier. Its upper branch, from the portfolio of smallest variance upward, is
the **efficient frontier**: the set of portfolios no feasible portfolio
dominates. The lower branch is attainable but never chosen, because for each of
its points the upper branch offers more return at the same volatility.

### Two anchors with closed forms

Dropping the return constraint from @eq-09-problem leaves the **minimum-variance
portfolio**, the single portfolio that minimizes variance subject only to being
fully invested:

$$
\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{mv}}
= \frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}}.
$$ {#eq-09-gmv}

Note what is absent: $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ does not appear. The minimum-variance
portfolio is the one point on the frontier that requires no view on expected
returns at all, and that fact will do a great deal of work later in this chapter.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: two assets, by hand

With $N = 2$ the matrix algebra of @eq-09-gmv collapses to a formula anyone can
evaluate on paper. Writing $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$ for the two volatilities and
$\sigma_{12} = \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ for the covariance,

$$
w_1 = \frac{\sigma_2^2 - \sigma_{12}}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\sigma_{12}},
\qquad w_2 = 1 - w_1 .
$$ {#eq-09-two-asset}

Take the two series a textbook would reach for, `US_equity` and
`US_government`, one with a high volatility and one with a low one. Their
annualized sample moments are


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pair <- c("US_equity", "US_government")
X    <- Re[, pair]

s1  <- stats::sd(X[, 1]) * sqrt(12)          # equity volatility
s2  <- stats::sd(X[, 2]) * sqrt(12)          # government volatility
rho <- stats::cor(X)[1, 2]
s12 <- rho * s1 * s2

w1       <- (s2^2 - s12) / (s1^2 + s2^2 - 2 * s12)
port_vol <- sqrt(w1^2 * s1^2 + (1 - w1)^2 * s2^2 + 2 * w1 * (1 - w1) * s12)

round(c(sigma_equity = s1, sigma_government = s2,
        correlation = rho, covariance = s12), 4)
#>     sigma_equity sigma_government      correlation       covariance 
#>           0.1562           0.0475          -0.1370          -0.0010
```
:::


so that $\sigma_1 = 0.1562$, $\sigma_2 = 0.0475$
and $\sigma_{12} = -0.1370 \times 0.1562 \times
0.0475 = -0.00102$. Substituting into
@eq-09-two-asset,

$$
w_1 = \frac{0.00226 - -0.00102}
           {0.02439 + 0.00226 - 2 \times -0.00102}
    = 0.1142,
\qquad
w_2 = 1 - w_1 = 0.8858,
$$

and the volatility of that portfolio, from @eq-09-moments with two assets, is

$$
\sigma_{\boldsymbol{w}}
= \sqrt{w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2 w_1 w_2 \sigma_{12}}
= \sqrt{0.00032 + 0.00177
        + -0.00021}
= 0.0434 .
$$

The same arithmetic in code, so that the numbers above are computed rather than
typed:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(c(w_equity = w1, w_government = 1 - w1,
        portfolio_vol = port_vol,
        lowest_vol_constituent = min(s1, s2),
        discount = port_vol / min(s1, s2) - 1), 4)
#>               w_equity           w_government          portfolio_vol 
#>                 0.1142                 0.8858                 0.0434 
#> lowest_vol_constituent               discount 
#>                 0.0475                -0.0866
```
:::


The portfolio has a lower volatility than either asset it holds, at
4.34% against
4.75% for the less volatile constituent. That
is the whole of diversification in one number, and it happens because
$\sigma_{12}$ is negative: the cross term in
@eq-09-moments subtracts where the two variances add.

Everything depends on the correlation, and the classic exhibit is to vary it
while holding both volatilities fixed.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
vary_rho <- function(r) {
  cv <- r * s1 * s2
  w  <- (s2^2 - cv) / (s1^2 + s2^2 - 2 * cv)
  c(rho = r, w_equity = w,
    portfolio_vol = sqrt(w^2 * s1^2 + (1 - w)^2 * s2^2 + 2 * w * (1 - w) * cv))
}

round(t(vapply(c(-1, -0.5, 0, rho, 0.5, 0.9, 1), vary_rho, numeric(3))), 4)
#>         rho w_equity portfolio_vol
#> [1,] -1.000   0.2334           NaN
#> [2,] -0.500   0.1753        0.0348
#> [3,]  0.000   0.0848        0.0455
#> [4,] -0.137   0.1142        0.0434
#> [5,]  0.500  -0.0755        0.0464
#> [6,]  0.900  -0.3328        0.0281
#> [7,]  1.000  -0.4376        0.0000
```
:::


Read the ends first. At $\rho = -1$ and at $\rho = +1$ the attainable volatility
is zero, because two perfectly correlated assets can be combined into a riskless
position: one long pair at $\rho = -1$, and a long-short pair at $\rho = +1$,
which is why the equity weight turns negative there. Between those extremes the
benefit shrinks as $\rho$ rises. At the measured correlation of
-0.14 a small part of it is left: the portfolio's volatility
is 8.7% below that of the
less volatile asset.

Two lessons carry into the sixteen-asset case. The riskless combinations at
$\rho = \pm 1$ are the two-asset version of @eq-07-riskless: when the covariance
matrix is singular, some combination has an estimated variance of exactly zero,
and an optimizer will find it. And @eq-09-two-asset needs no positivity: at
$\rho = +1$ it shorts, which is the closed form behaving exactly as it does on
sixteen assets, where it wants to short
5 of them.

Finally, the scalar formula and the matrix formula are the same statement, so
they must agree.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
S2   <- stats::cov(X) * 12
i2   <- rep(1, 2)
w_mx <- as.numeric(solve(S2) %*% i2) / as.numeric(t(i2) %*% solve(S2) %*% i2)

stopifnot(all.equal(w1, w_mx[1]))
round(c(by_hand = w1, by_matrix = w_mx[1]), 8)
#>   by_hand by_matrix 
#>    0.1142    0.1142
```
:::


The `stopifnot()` is not decoration. It is the cheapest possible guard that the
hand version and the matrix version have not drifted apart, and it fails the
render rather than printing a wrong number.
:::

If a risk-free asset is available, @tobin1958 showed that the investor's problem
separates. Every efficient portfolio is a combination of the risk-free asset and
one single risky portfolio, the same one for every investor regardless of risk
aversion. That portfolio is the **tangency portfolio**, and when returns are
measured in excess of the risk-free rate it is

$$
\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{tan}}
= \frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}.
$$ {#eq-09-tangency}

It is the portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio [@sharpe1966], the point at
which a ray from the risk-free rate touches the frontier. Two-fund separation is
what allows @sharpe1964 to move from an individual's portfolio problem to a
market equilibrium, and @roll1977 is the reminder that testing the resulting
model requires identifying that portfolio, which is harder than it looks.

The frontier itself has a closed form, due to @merton1972. Defining the three
scalars $A = \boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}$,
$B = \boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and
$C = \boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}$, the minimum
variance attainable at expected return $\bar{\mu}$ is

$$
\sigma^2(\bar{\mu}) = \frac{A\bar{\mu}^2 - 2B\bar{\mu} + C}{AC - B^2},
$$ {#eq-09-frontier}

a parabola in mean-variance space and a hyperbola in mean-standard-deviation
space. The minimum-variance portfolio sits at its vertex with variance $1/A$, and
the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio is $\sqrt{C}$. Derivations of
@eq-09-gmv through @eq-09-frontier are in @sec-91-proofs.

### Why the closed forms are not what we compute

Every expression above assumes weights may take any sign and any size. Real
mandates do not permit that, and the moment a short-sale constraint
$\boldsymbol{w} \geq \boldsymbol{0}$ is added, the closed form disappears.
@eq-09-problem becomes a quadratic program with inequality constraints, which has
no analytic solution but is convex and therefore solvable to numerical precision
in milliseconds [@boyd2004]. Everything computed in this chapter is a quadratic
program of that kind; @sec-13-solvers-theory is about the machinery.

There is a second, deeper reason the closed forms are a poor guide to practice.
They treat $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ as known, when in
application both are estimates, produced by the methods of
@sec-06-expected-returns-theory and @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory and carrying
the errors those chapters measure. @jobson1980 showed how badly the resulting
weights are estimated, and @best1991 traced the mechanism: because @eq-09-tangency
premultiplies $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ by $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, small changes in
estimated means produce large changes in weights, and the effect grows as the
covariance matrix becomes more nearly singular. @chopra1993 put a price on it,
finding errors in expected returns roughly an order of magnitude more costly than
errors in variances. @michaud1989 named the consequence: an optimizer is an
error-maximizer, systematically overweighting whatever the sample happened to
flatter.

That literature frames the rest of this chapter. We compute the textbook answer
in @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, and then in
@sec-09-mean-variance-application we measure how much of it is real.

## Implementation {#sec-09-mean-variance-implementation}

### Looking at the inputs first

Mean-variance consumes exactly two numbers per asset and one per pair. On this
panel those numbers are lopsided, and it is worth seeing how lopsided before any
optimizer runs.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ann_ret <- function(x) prod(1 + x)^(12 / length(x)) - 1
ann_vol <- function(x) stats::sd(x) * sqrt(12)

moments <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = colnames(R),
  mean_arith = apply(R, 2, mean) * 12,
  mean_comp  = apply(R, 2, ann_ret),
  vol        = apply(R, 2, ann_vol)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap = mean_arith - mean_comp,      # between the two annual figures
                half_var = vol^2 / 2) |>           # the drag of chapter 3, per year
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(mean_comp))
stopifnot(all(moments$gap > 0), all(moments$gap < moments$half_var))

vol_spread <- max(moments$vol) / min(moments$vol)
mean_cor   <- mean(stats::cor(R)[upper.tri(stats::cor(R))])
c(vol_spread = vol_spread, mean_correlation = mean_cor)
#>       vol_spread mean_correlation 
#>           4.4141           0.3367
```
:::


The most volatile series is 4.4 times the least, and
the average pairwise correlation is 0.34. Both numbers
constrain what the frontier can do, and @sec-09-mean-variance-application returns
to them.

The table carries two definitions of an average return. The arithmetic mean is
what enters $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, because variance is defined around it; the
compounded figure is what an investor actually earns over the period. Per period
the two differ by the variance drag of @eq-03-drag, half the variance. Between
the two annualized figures of the table the gap is smaller than half the annual
variance in every one of the 16 series, because twelve compounded
months also earn return on return, which works in the other direction. For
`EU_equity`, the series with the highest return,
the gap is 1.42 percentage points a year
against half a variance of 2.23. On the
more volatile series it is not a rounding artifact on either count.


::: {#tbl-09-drag .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Where the two definitions of an average return disagree most, with half the annual variance beside the gap. The gap is the price of volatility rather than a rounding artifact, and it falls short of half the variance because twelve compounded months add return on return.'}

|CH_equity |     11.94%|     10.75%|     18.25%| 1.19%|             1.66%|

A useful diagnostic before optimizing is to ask how many assets could possibly be
held. An asset is dominated in sample if some other asset offers a weakly higher
mean at a weakly lower volatility.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# j dominates i if it has a weakly higher mean and a weakly lower volatility.
# A sample statement with no test attached: it says what happened, not what
# will happen.
dominated <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(moments)), function(i) {
  any(moments$mean_comp >= moments$mean_comp[i] &
      moments$vol       <= moments$vol[i] &
      seq_len(nrow(moments)) != i)
}, logical(1))

moments$asset[dominated]
#>  [1] "UK_equity"        "CH_equity"        "JP_equity"        "UK_credit"       
#>  [5] "CH_credit"        "EU_credit"        "GLOBAL_commodity" "CH_government"   
#>  [9] "UK_government"    "EU_government"    "JP_credit"        "JP_government"
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_dominating <- function(i) sum(moments$mean_comp >= moments$mean_comp[i] &
                                moments$vol       <= moments$vol[i]) - 1L
by_how_many <- setNames(vapply(seq_len(nrow(moments)), n_dominating, integer(1)),
                        moments$asset)
sort(by_how_many[by_how_many > 0], decreasing = TRUE)
#>        JP_credit        JP_equity GLOBAL_commodity    JP_government 
#>                5                4                4                4 
#>    EU_government        CH_equity        EU_credit    CH_government 
#>                3                2                2                2 
#>    UK_government        UK_equity        UK_credit        CH_credit 
#>                2                1                1                1
```
:::


12 of 16 series are dominated, in the sense of
@sec-09-mean-variance-theory, by at least one other, and
JP_credit is dominated by 5 of the
15 alternatives. The efficient assets, the ones nothing
dominates, are `EU_equity`, `US_equity`, `US_credit`, `US_government`.
This is a statement about the sample and not a prediction, but it is visible
without an optimizer, and a reader who cannot see it in @fig-09-mu-sigma will not
see it in a weight vector either.

### Specifying and solving the problem

`PortfolioAnalytics` separates the description of a problem from its solution. A
`portfolio.spec` object collects the assets, the constraints and the objectives;
`optimize.portfolio()` then hands that specification to a solver. The
minimum-variance problem of @eq-09-gmv, with the short-sale constraint that
removes its closed form, is four lines.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>   # weights sum to one
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")            # 0 <= w <= 1

min_var_spec <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

w_gmv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, min_var_spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
round(w_gmv[w_gmv > 0.005], 4)
#>        EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity        JP_equity        UK_equity 
#>           0.0138           0.0507           0.0415           0.0218 
#>        US_equity    US_government 
#>           0.0513           0.8209
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
S <- stats::cov(Re)
mu <- colMeans(Re)
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w) p_ret(w) / p_vol(w)

c(volatility = p_vol(w_gmv), excess_return = p_ret(w_gmv), sharpe = p_sr(w_gmv))
#>    volatility excess_return        sharpe 
#>       0.04133       0.03286       0.79513
```
:::


The solution holds 6 of the sixteen series and places
82% of the money in
US_government. This is not a subtle allocation, and it is worth
being clear about why it happens. The least volatile series has an annualized
volatility of 4.8% against
7.3% for the next; minimizing
variance under a long-only constraint means buying the least volatile asset and
adding only whatever reduces the total further.

Concentration of this kind is often read as evidence that the estimates are bad.
@green1992 argue the opposite: extreme weights are what mean-variance optimization
produces whenever returns share a dominant common factor, whether or not the
inputs are well estimated. Whether this universe has such a factor is a measured
question rather than an assumption, and
@sec-05-factor-models-implementation answered it: one factor explains the four
developed equity blocks and almost nothing else. @clarke2011 derive the composition of the
minimum-variance portfolio explicitly and show that it holds few names by
construction. The concentration here is a property of the problem, not a symptom.

### The tangency portfolio

The maximum-Sharpe portfolio of @eq-09-tangency is the point where a ray from the
risk-free rate touches the frontier. `PortfolioAnalytics` offers `maxSR = TRUE`
for it, and the callout below explains why this book does not use it. The
portable route is to compute the frontier and read the best point off it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ef_spec <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

ef <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, ef_spec, type = "mean-StdDev", n.portfolios = 200)

# `ef$frontier` is a matrix carrying a class attribute, and `as.data.frame()`
# dispatches on that class: it returns every cell in a single column rather
# than one row of 19 per frontier portfolio. Strip the class first, or index it
# as the matrix it is.
fr <- as.data.frame(unclass(ef$frontier))
stopifnot(ncol(fr) == ncol(Re) + 3L)

# Returns are already in excess of the bill, so the Sharpe ratio is the ratio
# itself: no risk-free rate to subtract.
fr$sharpe <- fr$mean / fr$StdDev
i_tan <- which.max(fr$sharpe)

wcols <- grep("^w[.]", colnames(fr))
w_tan <- setNames(as.numeric(fr[i_tan, wcols]), sub("^w[.]", "", colnames(fr)[wcols]))
w_tan <- w_tan[colnames(Re)]
round(w_tan[w_tan > 0.005], 4)
#>        EU_equity GLOBAL_commodity        US_equity    US_government 
#>           0.0941           0.0311           0.1853           0.6853
```
:::

Two things matter later. The first is in @tbl-09-anchors: the tangency portfolio
has a Sharpe ratio 0.30 above that of
a naive 60/40 allocation, a wide margin and an entirely in-sample one. The second
is in the frontier the tangency portfolio was read from. The tangency portfolio
holds 0.4% in `US_credit`, and that
is where the series enters the frontier: to the left of the tangency point it is
held at no more than that, and to the right its weight grows to
17.5%. `US_credit` is the series with
the most negative skewness of the sixteen, at -1.45,
and the asymmetry is the work of a single month: without its worst month the
skewness is -0.10. The optimizer buys that
asymmetry because variance cannot see it: @eq-09-problem uses only the first two
moments. Changing the risk measure is not enough on its own, as
@sec-10-risk-measures-application shows: a tail measure estimated from the
historical returns does not see one month either, and only the moment-based
estimate of @sec-11-higher-moments-theory does. The example is not contrived. It
fell out of the standard procedure applied to the standard inputs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the closed form of @eq-09-gmv against the solver

@eq-09-gmv is an explicit formula, so we can evaluate it and compare. The
constants are those of @merton1972.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
iota <- rep(1, ncol(Re))
Sinv <- solve(S)

A <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% iota)
B <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% mu)
C <- as.numeric(t(mu)   %*% Sinv %*% mu)

w_gmv_cf <- setNames(as.numeric(Sinv %*% iota) / A, colnames(Re))
w_tan_cf <- setNames(as.numeric(Sinv %*% mu)   / B, colnames(Re))
```

### Three ways this fails without an error

Each of the following produces an object that looks like a solved portfolio.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The solver most examples use is the wrong one

Published examples commonly reach for `DEoptim`. That advice predates the convex
solvers in the package and is now not merely slow but wrong: minimum variance
under a budget and a sign constraint is a quadratic program, and a
differential-evolution search does not solve quadratic programs, it approximates
them. @sec-13-solvers-theory measures the approximation. On a problem with a
known answer the metaheuristics stop at roughly two thirds to three quarters of
the attainable Sharpe ratio after minutes of search, while `ROI` reaches all of
it in seconds. Use `ROI` for a
quadratic program, and reach for a metaheuristic only when the problem is
genuinely non-convex.
:::

The second failure concerns solver names. The modern incantation is
`optimize_method = c("CVXR", "OSQP")`, and the obvious reading of that vector is
wrong. Inside `optimize.portfolio()`:

```r
if (length(optimize_method) == 2)
  optimize_method <- optimize_method[2]
else optimize_method <- optimize_method[1]
```

The first element is discarded and dispatch happens on the second, matched
against a hard-coded list of names.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pa_cvxr_solvers <- c("CBC", "GLPK", "GLPK_MI", "OSQP", "CPLEX",
                     "SCS", "ECOS", "GUROBI", "MOSEK")
setdiff(CVXR::installed_solvers(), pa_cvxr_solvers)
#> [1] "CLARABEL" "HIGHS"
```
:::


`CLARABEL` is installed, is CVXR's own default interior-point solver, and is not
on that list. Asking for it raises nothing.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
opt_bad <- optimize.portfolio(Re, min_var_spec,
                              optimize_method = c("CVXR", "CLARABEL"))
c(class = class(opt_bad)[1],
  has_weights = !is.null(extractWeights(opt_bad)),
  elapsed = unname(opt_bad$elapsed_time))
#>                         class                   has_weights 
#> "optimize.portfolio.CLARABEL"                       "FALSE" 
#>                       elapsed 
#>         "0.00191092491149902"
```
:::


The call falls through every branch and returns a shell with a plausible class
and no weights. Inside a rebalancing loop that becomes a period of `NULL`, which
is the subject of @sec-25-backtesting-implementation. The guard is short and belongs in
anything that solves more than once.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
solve_checked <- function(R, spec, ...) {
  out <- optimize.portfolio(R, spec, ...)
  w <- extractWeights(out)
  if (is.null(w) || anyNA(w)) {
    cli::cli_abort(c(
      "The solver returned no usable weights.",
      "i" = "optimize.portfolio() returned an object of class {.cls {class(out)[1]}}.",
      ">" = "If you are using CVXR, the second element of {.arg optimize_method}
             must be one of {.val {pa_cvxr_solvers}}."
    ))
  }
  out
}

try(solve_checked(Re, min_var_spec, optimize_method = c("CVXR", "CLARABEL")))
#> Error in solve_checked(Re, min_var_spec, optimize_method = c("CVXR", "CLARABEL")) : 
#>   The solver returned no usable weights.
#> ℹ optimize.portfolio() returned an object of class
#>   <optimize.portfolio.CLARABEL>.
#> → If you are using CVXR, the second element of `optimize_method` must be one of
#>   "CBC", "GLPK", "GLPK_MI", "OSQP", "CPLEX", "SCS", "ECOS", "GUROBI", and
```

:::


::: {.callout-important}
## An exact budget constraint can be reported as infeasible

This guard catches a second failure that has nothing to do with solver names. On
the CRAN release of `PortfolioAnalytics`, an exact `full_investment` constraint
is encoded as two opposing inequality rows, which are simultaneously active and
linearly dependent. `quadprog` then reports the problem infeasible and ROI
returns `NA` weights without raising a condition. Measured on this data, that
fails in **30 of 312** rolling sixty-month minimum-variance windows, for a
constraint set consisting of nothing but $\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} = 1$
and $\boldsymbol{w} \geq \boldsymbol{0}$. The fix is recorded in
@sec-93-package-notes. Until it reaches CRAN, `solve_checked()` is what stands
between the reader and a backtest with holes in it.
:::

The third failure concerns return targets. A target can be attached to a
constraint or to the return objective, and the backends disagree about what the
second means.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
target_monthly <- as.numeric(quantile(mu, 0.75))

on_constraint <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = target_monthly) |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

on_objective <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean", target = target_monthly) |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

achieved <- function(spec, method) {
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = method))
  sum(w * mu)
}

trap <- tibble::tibble(
  route = c("constraint, ROI", "constraint, CVXR/OSQP",
            "objective, ROI",  "objective, CVXR/OSQP"),
  achieved = c(achieved(on_constraint, "ROI"),
               achieved(on_constraint, c("CVXR", "OSQP")),
               achieved(on_objective,  "ROI"),
               achieved(on_objective,  c("CVXR", "OSQP")))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(target = target_monthly,
                hit = abs(achieved - target) < 1e-8)
trap
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   route                 achieved  target hit  
#>   <chr>                    <dbl>   <dbl> <lgl>
#> 1 constraint, ROI        0.00554 0.00554 TRUE 
#> 2 constraint, CVXR/OSQP  0.00554 0.00554 TRUE 
#> 3 objective, ROI         0.00554 0.00554 TRUE 
#> 4 objective, CVXR/OSQP   0.0103  0.00554 FALSE

# What the fourth route solved instead: the same two objectives with the target
# removed, which is quadratic utility at the default risk aversion of one.
no_target <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
stopifnot(trap$hit[1:3], !trap$hit[4],
          isTRUE(all.equal(trap$achieved[4], achieved(no_target, "ROI"),
                           tolerance = 1e-6)))
```
:::


Under `ROI` the objective's `target` is honored. Under `CVXR` it is read only
when `optimize.portfolio()` is called internally with `ef = TRUE`, which happens
from `meanvar.efficient.frontier()` and nowhere else. On a direct call the target
is dropped and the solver maximizes quadratic utility at the default risk
aversion instead, silently: the assertion that closes the chunk confirms that it
returns the portfolio of the same two objectives with no target at all. Put the
target on the constraint: it is the portable form, and it is the one that means
what it says.

line and the tangency point in a single call, and it locates the tangency

than by calling `maxSR`.

## What the Frontier Actually Buys {#sec-09-mean-variance-application}

### The frontier is a set of answers, not an object

There is no single problem whose solution is the efficient frontier. There are as
many problems as there are points, each a separate quadratic program with its own
target return, and the frontier is where their answers landed.

Everything a textbook draws on that picture can be produced from
`PortfolioAnalytics`, and none of it is as obvious as the theory makes it look.
The frontier comes from `create.EfficientFrontier()`, the tangency has to be read
off it rather than requested, the quadratic-utility portfolios come from a risk
objective carrying a `risk_aversion` argument, and the capital allocation line is
not a function the package offers at all. We compute each here.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Quadratic utility: maximize mu'w - lambda * w'Sigma w. In PortfolioAnalytics
# this is a return objective plus a risk objective carrying `risk_aversion`.
# Note that `risk_aversion` is gamma/2, not gamma -- see appendix B.
qu_weights <- function(lambda) {
  spec <- base_spec |>
    add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = lambda)
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

lambdas <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 25)
w_qu <- lapply(lambdas, qu_weights)
names(w_qu) <- sprintf("lambda = %g", lambdas)

vapply(w_qu, function(w) c(vol = p_vol(w), ret = p_ret(w)), numeric(2)) |> round(4)
#>     lambda = 1 lambda = 2 lambda = 5 lambda = 10 lambda = 25
#> vol      0.167     0.1448     0.0707      0.0507      0.0430
#> ret      0.124     0.1126     0.0664      0.0502      0.0399
```
:::


Raising `risk_aversion` walks the solution leftward along the frontier, which is
the statement of @sec-91-proofs-quadratic-utility made numerically: each
$\lambda$ selects one frontier point, and the map is monotone.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The capital allocation line. Returns here are already in excess of the bill,
# so the risk-free asset sits at the origin and a mix of a in the tangency
# portfolio and 1-a in the bill is simply a scalar multiple of it.
a <- seq(0, 1.6, by = 0.2)
cal <- tibble::tibble(
  label = sprintf("%.0f%% risky", 100 * a),
  vol   = a * p_vol(w_tan),
  ret   = a * p_ret(w_tan),
  kind  = "capital allocation line"
)
```
:::

data frame before anything is drawn. Building a plot from parallel vectors is how
a volatility ends up next to the wrong return, which is a mistake this chapter
made until it started labeling its own points.

Three things in @fig-09-frontier are worth stating, because each is a place where
the theory is easy and the implementation is not.

The quadratic-utility diamonds lie **on** the frontier rather than near it. That
is the check that the objective was specified correctly: if `risk_aversion` is
passed to the wrong objective, or the return objective is omitted, the solution
still returns weights and still plots, but it lands off the curve.

The capital allocation line passes through the origin rather than through a
risk-free rate on the vertical axis, because these returns are already in excess
of the bill. Plotting total returns instead moves the intercept to the bill's
return and changes which frontier point is tangent. This is the single most
common way the picture comes out wrong.

The tangency point is the one place the line touches the curve, and it was found
by scanning the frontier for the highest Sharpe ratio rather than by asking for
it. `maxSR = TRUE` exists and does not do this reliably, which is
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation's subject.

### The left end is stable and the right end is not

@eq-09-gmv depends only on $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$; every point to the right of the
vertex depends on $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ as well. Means are estimated far less
precisely than variances from the same sample, a point
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation measured directly: the rolling mean wanders
by more than its own level while volatility moves by roughly a third of its own.
The theoretical consequence is @best1991; the practical one can be shown with a
resampling experiment.

We draw the same thirty-one model years in twelve-month blocks, which preserves
the serial dependence a naive bootstrap would destroy [@kuensch1989; @politis1994],
re-optimize on each draw, and measure how far the answer moves from the
full-sample one.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)

block_index <- function(n, block = 12L) {
  starts <- sample.int(n - block + 1L, ceiling(n / block), replace = TRUE)
  as.vector(outer(0:(block - 1L), starts, "+"))[seq_len(n)]
}

# Half the L1 distance between two long-only weight vectors: the share of the
# portfolio that must change hands to get from one to the other. The guard is
# not decoration -- given NULL, the unguarded arithmetic returns zero, and a
# failed solve would enter the sample as a portfolio that did not move.
turnover <- function(w1, w2) {
  if (is.null(w1) || is.null(w2)) stop("a failed solve is not a turnover of zero")
  sum(abs(w1[names(w2)] - w2)) / 2
}

B <- 200L
boot <- vapply(seq_len(B), function(b) {
  Rb <- xts::xts(zoo::coredata(Re)[block_index(nrow(Re)), ], order.by = zoo::index(Re))
  wg <- extractWeights(solve_checked(Rb, min_var_spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
  fb <- as.data.frame(unclass(
    create.EfficientFrontier(Rb, ef_spec, type = "mean-StdDev",
                             n.portfolios = 60)$frontier))
  wt <- setNames(as.numeric(fb[which.max(fb$mean / fb$StdDev), wcols]),
                 sub("^w[.]", "", colnames(fb)[wcols]))
  c(gmv = turnover(wg[colnames(Re)], w_gmv),
    tangency = turnover(wt[colnames(Re)], w_tan))
}, numeric(2))
```

### Diversification effort and diversification payoff are unrelated

It is tempting to attribute the minimum-variance portfolio's low volatility to
diversification. Mostly it is not diversification at all.

The cleanest way to see this is to run the same construction on two universes,
one built to be heterogeneous and one built to be homogeneous. The sixteen
classes span bonds, equities and commodities. The five equity classes are the
same asset in five places.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
Req <- Re[, grepl("_equity$", colnames(Re))]
Ceq <- stats::cor(Req)
Seq <- stats::cov(Req)

w_gmv_eq <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Req,
  portfolio.spec(colnames(Req)) |>
    add.constraint("full_investment") |> add.constraint("long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
  optimize_method = "ROI"))

# Effective bets: the reciprocal of the Herfindahl index of the weights. Sixteen
# equal positions score 16, everything in one name scores 1. It counts positions
# the way an investor would, not the way the weight vector's length does.
eff_bets <- function(w) 1 / sum(w^2)

vol_eq <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(w_gmv_eq) %*% Seq %*% w_gmv_eq)) * sqrt(12)

# The comparison the text draws, asserted: the equity portfolio holds more
# effective positions and lands no further below its least volatile constituent.
stopifnot(eff_bets(w_gmv_eq) > eff_bets(w_gmv),
          vol_eq / min(apply(Req, 2, ann_vol)) > p_vol(w_gmv) / min(moments$vol))

tibble::tibble(
  universe         = c("16 mixed classes", "5 equity classes"),
  mean_correlation = c(mean_cor, mean(Ceq[upper.tri(Ceq)])),
  gmv_vol          = c(p_vol(w_gmv), vol_eq),
  lowest_vol_asset = c(min(moments$vol), min(apply(Req, 2, ann_vol))),
  effective_bets   = c(eff_bets(w_gmv), eff_bets(w_gmv_eq))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gain = gmv_vol / lowest_vol_asset - 1)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   universe       mean_correlation gmv_vol lowest_vol_asset effective_bets   gain
#>   <chr>                     <dbl>   <dbl>            <dbl>          <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 16 mixed clas…            0.337  0.0413           0.0478           1.47 -0.136
#> 2 5 equity clas…            0.548  0.138            0.156            3.49 -0.114
```
:::


The count of effective bets above is the reciprocal of the Herfindahl index of
the weights, the simplest of several measures of how concentrated a portfolio
really is [@choueifaty2008; @meucci2009].

The two universes could hardly be less alike. Average pairwise correlation is
0.34 across the classes and
0.55 within equities. What the
optimizer does with them differs accordingly: across the classes it holds
1.47 effective positions out of sixteen, because
82% of the portfolio is `US_government`.
Among equities, where no series has a low volatility, it has no such option and holds
3.49 of five.

One of those is barely a portfolio and the other is a real one. Now compare what
each bought. Minimum variance lands
13.6% below the
least volatile class series, and
11.4% below the
least volatile equity market. The portfolio with
2.4 times the effective
positions buys the smaller discount.

### Five hundred universes, one constant

Two universes are suggestive and no more. If the minimum-variance level really is
set by what is available rather than by how it combines, the pattern should hold
on universes nobody designed.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)

gmv_vol_of <- function(X) {
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X,
    portfolio.spec(colnames(X)) |>
      add.constraint("full_investment") |> add.constraint("long_only") |>
      add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
    optimize_method = "ROI"))
  sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% stats::cov(X) %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
}

draws <- lapply(3:16, function(n) {
  lapply(seq_len(if (n == 16) 1 else 40), function(...) {
    X <- Re[, sort(sample.int(ncol(Re), n))]
    C <- stats::cor(X)
    data.frame(n = n, mean_cor = mean(C[upper.tri(C)]),
               gmv_vol = gmv_vol_of(X), min_vol = min(apply(X, 2, ann_vol)))
  })
})
subu <- do.call(rbind, unlist(draws, recursive = FALSE)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gain = gmv_vol / min_vol - 1)

c(universes = nrow(subu),
  median_gain = median(subu$gain),
  worst_gain = min(subu$gain),
  best_gain = max(subu$gain))
#>   universes median_gain  worst_gain   best_gain 
#>   521.00000    -0.12928    -0.29403    -0.01283
```
:::


Across 521 sub-universes drawn from the same sixteen series, the
median portfolio lands 12.9% below its
own least volatile constituent; the smallest discount is
1% and the largest is
29%. The size of the discount depends on
the selection, then. Where the level comes from does not.

Which of the two inputs decides the level?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
r2 <- function(f) summary(stats::lm(f, data = subu))$r.squared

c(lowest_vol_alone    = r2(log(gmv_vol) ~ log(min_vol)),
  correlation_alone    = r2(log(gmv_vol) ~ mean_cor),
  everything           = r2(log(gmv_vol) ~ log(min_vol) + mean_cor + n))
#>  lowest_vol_alone correlation_alone        everything 
#>           0.97673           0.05067           0.98840
```
:::


The volatility of the least volatile available asset explains
98% of the variation in
the minimum-variance level. Average correlation, which is what the word
diversification refers to, explains
5%. Both together with the
size of the universe reach
99%.

This deserves stating plainly, because the claim that diversification is the only
free lunch is usually offered as though the combining did the work. On this
evidence it does not. Choosing the universe fixes the answer to within the
discount, typically 13% and never
more than 29% here, and the optimizer
then allocates inside a room whose ceiling was fixed before it was called. That is the first argument in this book for spending effort
on which assets are eligible rather than on the machinery that weights them, and
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory returns to it.

### What each constraint costs

A mandate is a sequence of restrictions, and each one moves the frontier
south-east. Running the same problem four times makes the cost of each visible
rather than asserted.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
group_of <- function(a) dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", a)     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", a) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", a)     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                     ~ "commodity")
# split() returns its groups in alphabetical order, so the limit vectors below
# are built by name rather than positionally. Getting that wrong applies the
# equity limit to the commodity and nothing complains.
grp <- split(seq_len(ncol(Re)), group_of(colnames(Re)))
gmin <- c(commodity = 0.00, credit = 0.05, equity = 0.20, government = 0.10)
gmax <- c(commodity = 0.15, credit = 0.40, equity = 0.60, government = 0.50)
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(gmin)))

spec_unconstrained <- portfolio.spec(colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = -1, max = 1) |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

spec_box <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.25) |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

spec_group <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.25) |>
  add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp,
                 group_min = unname(gmin[names(grp)]),
                 group_max = unname(gmax[names(grp)])) |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")

ladder <- list(`1 no short-sale limit` = spec_unconstrained,
               `2 long only`           = ef_spec,
               `3 plus a 25% cap`      = spec_box,
               `4 plus group limits`   = spec_group)

fronts <- lapply(names(ladder), function(nm) {
  e <- create.EfficientFrontier(Re, ladder[[nm]], type = "mean-StdDev",
                                n.portfolios = 100)
  f <- as.data.frame(unclass(e$frontier))
  data.frame(spec = nm, vol = f$StdDev * sqrt(12), ret = f$mean * 12,
             sharpe = f$mean / f$StdDev)
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
```

### And it does not survive contact with the future

Everything above is in sample. Running the same portfolios out of sample, with a
sixty-month rolling estimate and monthly rebalancing, takes the tangency
portfolio from first place to last. The
out-of-sample column is read from the register that @sec-25-backtesting-application
computes, rather than recomputed here, so that the two chapters cannot drift
apart.


::: {#tbl-09-oos .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The same three portfolios, estimated on the full sample and estimated on a sixty-month rolling window. Only the second column is achievable.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|portfolio        | in_sample| out_of_sample|  kept|
|:----------------|---------:|-------------:|-----:|
|Tangency         |     0.991|         0.546| 0.551|
|Minimum variance |     0.795|         0.829| 1.043|
|Equal weight     |     0.617|         0.626| 1.015|


:::

The tangency portfolio keeps 55%
of the Sharpe ratio it promised and finishes last of the three. Minimum
variance, which needed no estimate of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ at all, keeps
104%, and equal weighting, which
promised the least, keeps 102%; a
share above 100% is possible because the out-of-sample record covers model years
11 to 31 rather than the
whole sample. Two rules deliver what the full sample said they would, and the one
that estimates the mean does not.

The order of the three depends on the estimation window. With 120 months behind
each estimate instead of sixty, the tangency portfolio reaches a Sharpe ratio of
0.70 and finishes ahead of equal weighting at
0.63, though behind minimum variance at
0.91. What does not depend on the window, or
on how often the portfolio is rebalanced, is the following. In every cell of the
register, with windows of 36, 60 and 120 months and monthly, quarterly and annual
rebalancing, minimum variance has the highest Sharpe ratio of the three, and the
tangency portfolio keeps the smallest share of what it promised, between
35% and
76%. This is the pattern
@demiguel2009 report for fourteen rules on seven datasets: none was consistently
better than equal weighting out of sample, the failure was attributable to
estimation error rather than to any defect in @eq-09-problem itself, and the
estimation window a mean-based rule needs before it does better is long, which
is the direction of the 120-month result here. @jagannathan2003
explain why minimum variance is the exception: dropping the mean removes the
input that is estimated worst.

At the sixty-month window the portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio in this
chapter has the lowest of the 5 strategies in the register of
@sec-25-backtesting-application. The gap between the two columns of @tbl-09-oos
is the subject of the rest of the book.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- Mean-variance optimization has a closed-form solution only when weights are
  unconstrained. Adding a short-sale constraint turns @eq-09-problem into a
  quadratic program, which is what every result in this chapter actually solves.
- The minimum-variance portfolio of @eq-09-gmv does not involve expected returns.
  That makes it the one point on the frontier requiring no return forecast, and
  it is why it is far more stable than the tangency portfolio.
- Concentration is not automatically a symptom of bad estimates. A dominant
  common factor produces concentrated efficient portfolios even with perfect
  inputs [@green1992; @clarke2011].
- The left end of the frontier is determined by $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and the
  right end by $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, which is estimated far less precisely. A block
  bootstrap makes the tangency portfolio move several times as far as the
  minimum-variance portfolio on the same data.
- The level of minimum variance is set mainly by the least volatile asset
  available, not by how assets combine. Universe selection matters more than the weighting
  machinery applied afterwards.
- In sample the tangency portfolio has the highest Sharpe ratio by construction;
  out of sample it keeps the smallest share of what it promised at every
  estimation window. It finishes behind minimum variance throughout, and behind
  equal weighting at the sixty-month window though not at 120 months
  [@demiguel2009; @jagannathan2003].
